title: Here’s How We Can Turn the Tide on the Dating Recession
author: Andrea Gurney
summary: Clinical psychologist Andrea Gurney draws on the IFS and Wheatley Institute report The Dating Recession to argue that young adults still want marriage but are stuck between aspiration and action. Roughly 70 percent of those who say they want to marry are barely dating, which she calls a crisis of design rather than desire. She traces the problem to a consumer mindset shaped by apps and choice overload, to soulmate myths that make friction look like failure, and to a relationship-education field that neglected how couples actually get started. Only one in three young men and one in five young women feel confident approaching someone in person. In response she introduces the Dating Education Action Network, a working group of educators, clinicians, researchers and faith leaders aiming to shift the culture, build curricula and create real-world social pathways for dating.
points: Most young adults still expect to marry, so the dating recession is better understood as a gap between desire and the skills and settings needed to act on it.
Dating apps encourage a consumer model of relationships in which partners are products to be evaluated and discarded, in contrast to a covenantal view of commitment.
Soulmate and destiny beliefs make ordinary friction look like proof that someone is not the one, pushing people toward ambiguity such as situationships.
Relationship education has focused on engaged and married couples and left the initiation stage to algorithms and hookup culture.
Remedies include a character-first framework for partnership, research-based dating curricula and local community pathways where young adults can meet in person.
quotes: Here lies the great paradox of our time: We are living through a historic dating recession, but it is a crisis of design, not of desire. Nearly 70% of young adults who say they want to marry are not actively dating; they are going out only a few times a year, or not at all.

Sociologists call this commodification—the shift from a covenantal view of relationships to a consumeristic one. In a covenantal model, partners are viewed as unique, irreplaceable human beings, bound by a commitment that transcends shifting feelings.

Think about how we shop online: If we buy a sweater and notice a single loose thread, we don't try to repair it—we send it back because there are ten thousand other sweaters on that digital storefront (and free shipping, too).
In a world of infinite swipes, they’ve stopped looking for reasons to stay in relationships and find themselves attuned to the tiniest excuse to leave.

So, many young adults begin to believe that true compatibility should be effortless. If friction arises—which it inevitably does in any human connection—they think, “This must not be ‘The One,’” and head for the exit.

We left the critical stage of dating initiation and marriage formation almost entirely to commercial algorithms and hookup culture. As a result, today’s young adults suffer from an acute skills and confidence deficit.
Young adults do not need better algorithms. They need the courage to tolerate human imperfection, the tools to communicate clearly, and the cultural permission to choose commitment over convenience.
